extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers interested in Civil War-era press behavior
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for assessing 19th-century American newspapers during the Civil War and Reconstruction era — including loyalty, editorial quality, news enterprise, censorship, partisanship, and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loyalty to the Union versus disloyalty/southern sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a paper was 'loyal' to the Union and supported the administration or sympathized with/seized positions favorable to the South or secession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout the chapter to classify papers (e.g., Herald 'after Sumter the Herald was a loyal paper' but also bludgeoned Lincoln; many Democratic papers were not disloyal; some Republican papers distrusted Lincoln). Loyalty influenced distribution rights, suppression, and public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for emancipation / treatment of slavery question
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper's stance on slavery and emancipation — e.g., strong demands for emancipation, rejoicing at the Emancipation Proclamation, or condemnation of the proclamation as 'fanatical, unconstitutional, and impossible to execute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper's position on emancipation marked its political alignment (radical, conservative, Peace Democrat) and affected readership and influence (Evening Post, Tribune, Liberator, Independent praised emancipation; World condemned it under Marble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and sincerity of editorial policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the paper maintained a coherent, consistent editorial line (consistency increases credibility and influence) or adopted inconsistent/tardy shifts that reduced influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Herald's inconsistent policy ('The paper’s policy was too inconsistent to make it influential: the readers of its editorials could not believe fully in its sincerity'). Inconsistency undermined readers' trust and editorial influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial tone and decorum (candid, courteous vs angry/vituperative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of editorial expression — a good political editor should be 'always candid and courteous, never angry or vituperative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style of expression was an explicit normative standard (Forney praised for candor and courtesy). Tone affected perceived professionalism and standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: News enterprise and reporting quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Breadth and vigor of news-gathering: exclusive bulletins, large/frequent war maps, good correspondence from battle fronts, and general news enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers with strong news enterprise gained readership and leadership (e.g., the Inquirer’s war maps and correspondence, Herald's 'news enterprise' giving it largest circulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and editorial care (avoid careless editing/forgeries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obligation to verify important documents and reports; careless editing / failure to verify can lead to serious consequences (government suppression, loss of mailing privileges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: World and Journal of Commerce printed a forged presidential proclamation and were suppressed; guidance: 'other papers ... suspected a “fake,” and attempted verification: the World and Journal were less careful, and suffered.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship, postal suspension, and government suppression as response
rubrics_metrics.description: Government actions (suppression, suspension from mails, imprisonment of editors) used as responses to perceived disloyalty or dangerous publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: World and Journal suppressed by General Dix; Postmaster General ordered papers not accepted for mailing; editors imprisoned (e.g., Freeman’s Journal editor McMaster). The text treats such suppression both as consequence and as indicator of perceived threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political alignment and advocacy role (party organ vs independent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a paper functioned as a party organ, an administration organ, an independent editorial voice, or a 'spokesman' for a wing of a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Times as a Seward paper but an 'individualistic' editor made it leading advocate of the administration; Forney’s Press was 'the chief Republican paper in Pennsylvania'; role affected editorial positions and political influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence and leadership (campaign leadership, election impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which an editor/paper exercises political leadership or influences campaigns and public opinion (e.g., chairing committees, organizing campaigns, soldier balloting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Henry J. Raymond chaired the national Republican committee and ran Lincoln’s re-election campaign; Medill advanced soldier balloting project; influence measured by political roles and campaign activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation, price, and distribution as measures of reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation numbers, price point, and special distribution (e.g., army distribution, weekly editions) used to measure reach and the paper's constituency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Inquirer circulation to 60,000 in 1862; Daily News claimed 'The Largest Circulation'; price changes (one cent to higher) and army distribution (War Press) influenced audience and financial viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism versus respectable journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Content quality spectrum from sensational, police-gazette-type news and advertising to serious, enterprising reporting and editorial standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daily News exemplified sensation: 'four pages of five columns... filled with sensational news of the police-gazette type' — considered lower journalistic standing despite high circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialized content (e.g., war maps, front correspondence) as journalistic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of features like large/frequent war maps and first-hand correspondence enhances a paper’s journalistic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philadelphia Inquirer praised for 'its war maps were the largest and most frequent... it had good correspondence from the battle fronts,' contributing to circulation growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being well-informed via authoritative correspondence (editorial generals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors maintaining correspondence with field officers and other authoritative sources ('editorial generals') were 'fairly well informed' and used that to shape editorial judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bryant and Parke Godwin corresponded with leading officers; being informed justified military-strategy critiques and lent weight to editorials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy for military policy (coercion vs conciliation; urging vigor or reorganization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers were judged by their advocacy for military approaches (coercion of seceded states, urging vigor, advocating reorganization of command) or for conciliation/compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Times stuck to coercion principle; many Republican papers urged vigor and reorganizations after defeats; stances reflected editorial philosophy and political strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: External pressures (mobs, threats) and their effect on editorial behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: How physical threats, mobs, and public pressure forced editorial gestures (e.g., hanging a flag) or affected continuity of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mob visited Herald demanding display of flag leading to policy shift; multiple papers' plants wrecked by mobs; threats influenced editorial choices and survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing legitimate criticism from treasonous support
rubrics_metrics.description: The normative distinction journalists debated: deny the press the right to 'uphold treason or rebellion' while affirming 'its right to criticize the acts of the government, both civil and military.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After suppression incidents, journalists (meeting chaired by Greeley) passed resolutions to that effect; this provides an ethical/constitutional standard for acceptable press behavior during war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copperhead identification formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria used to identify 'Copperhead' (anti-war / pro-peace-at-any-price) papers, listed as (1) magnify Confederate victories and depreciate Union ones, (2) parade reports from southern papers boasting their army, (3) calumniate efficient northern generals and laud incompetent ones, (4) seize upon a reverse to demand ending the war, (5) sneer at northern financial system, (6) abuse the President and cabinet without consistency or truth, (7) rail about the 'niggers' in the army, and (8) clamor against the draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the 'Copperhead formula' (quoted from New York Evening Post, May 20, 1863) — a checklist for spotting journals whose conduct was judged inimical to the Union war effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial leadership style and temperament (practical example: Forney)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities of an effective political editor: practical experience, candidness, courtesy, and the ability to coordinate editorial positions across presses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forney is described as 'a great political editor' who was 'always candid and courteous, never angry or vituperative.' His papers (Press and Chronicle) strongly supported Lincoln policies and distributed widely in the army.
